benchmark_name: DepressionAgent: Reading, Listening, Seeing, and Deliberating Multimodal Evidence for Depression Risk Assessment
authors: Fangjie Zhu; Haifeng Lu; Sicheng Zhao; Runhao Zeng; Xiping Hu
institutions: Shenzhen MSU-BIT University (Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Joint Laboratory for Emotional Intelligence and Pervasive Computing; Artificial Intelligence Research Institute); The University of Hong Kong; Tsinghua University
ground_truth_source: Dataset-defined binary depression risk labels from D-Vlog and LMVD public benchmarks; ground-truth labels accessed only after inference for metric computation
what_assessed_skills: Multimodal depression risk assessment via explicit evidence deliberation: modality-specific evidence extraction (text, audio, video); support–challenge reasoning; cross-modal arbitration; conflict reflection; risk-sensitive textual reassessment; explainability/inspectability of reasoning
tasks_assessed: Binary depression risk classification (depressed vs. not depressed) from multimodal video data; multimodal evidence extraction and deliberation; cross-modal conflict resolution; risk reflection for false-negative reduction
population_represented: YouTube vloggers (D-Vlog: 816 speakers, English vlogs); social media video participants (LMVD: 1,475 participants, multiple platforms); real-world unconstrained environments
evaluation_method: Automated evaluation on benchmark test sets using Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-score (positive class = depression risk); ablation studies; reflection transition analysis; language masking experiments. Human evaluation by 5 clinicians (2 junior, 3 senior psychiatrists) on 30 D-Vlog samples using 5-point Likert scale (Evidence Relevance, Reasoning Coherence, Clinical Utility) and binary reasonable/unreasonable judgments for structured reasoning operations; ICC and Fleiss' κ for inter-rater agreement. Evaluation: Both (Automated + Human).
performance_scores: D-Vlog (matched test set): Acc=95.26%, Prec=95.24%, Rec=96.15%, F1=95.69%. LMVD (matched test set): Acc=82.57%, Prec=80.48%, Rec=85.76%, F1=83.04%. Full D-Vlog pool: Acc=92.43%, F1=93.20%. Cross-model accuracy gains vs. direct prediction: Qwen3-Omni +20.1pp, GPT-5.5 +29.1pp, Gemini 3.1 Pro +20.7pp. Clinician Likert means: Evidence Relevance=3.65, Reasoning Coherence=3.71, Clinical Utility=3.21.
short_summary: DepressionAgent is an evidence-centric, reflection-driven multi-agent framework for multimodal depression risk assessment from text, audio, and video. Rather than fusing latent features, it explicitly extracts modality-specific evidence, organizes it into self-report and audio-visual behavioral branches with Hypothesis and Challenger agents, performs cross-modal arbitration with Conflict Reflection, and applies Risk Reflection for low-risk cases to reduce false negatives. The framework operates in a zero-shot, training-free setting using LLMs (default: Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct) and is evaluated on D-Vlog and LMVD benchmarks. It achieves state-of-the-art competitive performance (95.69% F1 on D-Vlog test set) and is additionally assessed by five clinicians for reasoning quality and inspectability.

benchmark_name: How LLMs Respond to Escalating Delusions: Four Longitudinal Trajectories of Model Behavior
authors: Anna Sterna; Kacper Dudzic; Karolina Drożdż; Hubert Plisiecki; Marcin Rządeczka; Marcin Moskalewicz
institutions: IDEAS Research Institute, Warsaw; Adam Mickiewicz University, Poznan; AMU Center for Artificial Intelligence, Poznan; Maria Curie-Skłodowska University, Lublin
ground_truth_source: Qualitative ratings by four trained psychology students using researcher-defined criteria (recognition stage, interpretative confidence, intervention profile, disengagement flag); criteria formulated by a clinical psychologist; adjudicated disengagement variable re-coded by an independent second coder on 20% subsample
size_of_benchmark: 449 model-days (15 models × 30 days, minus 1 missing response); 30-message scripted conversation
what_assessed_skills: LLM psychosis recognition timing and trajectory; clinical framing stability; intervention accuracy (education, psychoeducation, emotional support, psychological interpretation, recommendation); disengagement recommendation behavior; semantic entrainment to delusional content; interpretative confidence/modality; potential to exacerbate AI psychosis
tasks_assessed: Multi-turn scripted conversation with simulated prodromal psychotic user escalating over 30 days; recognition stage rating (naive engagement to stabilized clinical framing); intervention profile assessment; disengagement flag detection; automated entrainment scoring; automated modality (booster/hedge) scoring
population_represented: Simulated prodromal psychotic user (stressed, isolated, sleep-deprived); representative of individuals in prodromal phase of psychosis, including those vulnerable to AI psychosis
evaluation_method: Both (Human + Automated). Human: four trained psychology students rated all 449 model-days on recognition stage (4-point ordinal), interpretative confidence (3-point), and intervention profile (5 categories, 3-point Likert each); disengagement flag adjudicated by one adjudicator confirmed on 20% subsample by independent second coder. Metrics: Krippendorff's α, pairwise quadratic-weighted κ, ICC, permutation tests on rank-sums. Automated: two computational metrics — entrainment (cosine similarity of semantic embeddings, Qwen3-Embedding-4B) and modality (booster/hedge lexicon count via spaCy).
llms_evaluated: Claude Haiku 3.5, Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 3, Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.1, Claude Opus 4.5, GPT-4o, GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek-V3
mental_health_conditions: Psychosis (prodromal psychosis, AI psychosis, delusional beliefs, psychotic ideation)
performance_scores: Four trajectory regimes identified: (1) Premature medicalization/disengagement: Claude Haiku 4.5 (clinical framing day 3, stable day 5, first Level-B day 3, 26 days at stage 4, 28 Level-B days); (2) Recognition without safeguarding: GPT-5.1 Instant (clinical day 7, stable day 21, no Level-B), GPT-5.1 Thinking (clinical day 14, stable day 24, no Level-B); (3) Delayed/unstable recognition: Claude Opus 4.1 (day 21), Claude Haiku 3.5 (day 22), GPT-4o (day 22), Claude Opus 4 (day 24), Claude Opus 3 (day 26), Gemini 3.1 Pro (day 26); (4) Delusion co-construction — never reached clinical framing: Claude Sonnet 4, DeepSeek-V3, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro. Entrainment: 4.5-gen Claude lowest (0.05–0.14), never-turning models highest (0.21–0.25); correlated with Level-B counts (Spearman ρ=−.69, p=.005). Recognition stage ICC(2,k)=.948. Level-A recommendations: 118/449 days; Level-B: 93/449 days.
short_summary: This paper proposes and tests a longitudinal evaluation framework to assess how 15 mainstream LLMs respond to a simulated user progressively descending from mild anomalous experiences into psychotic ideation over 30 scripted messages. The study addresses the phenomenon of "AI psychosis" — where LLMs may act as catalysts or co-authors of delusional beliefs — and is the first to evaluate LLMs longitudinally across an extended interaction with a prodromal psychotic user, including the AI itself as an object of delusion. Four trained human evaluators rated all 449 model-days on recognition stage, interpretative confidence, and intervention profile, supplemented by two automated metrics (entrainment and modality). Four distinct trajectory regimes were identified across the 15 models: premature medicalization/disengagement (Claude Haiku 4.5), recognition without safeguarding (GPT-5.1 Instant/Thinking), delayed and unstable recognition (Claude Opus 3/4/4.1, Claude Haiku 3.5, GPT-4o, Gemini 3.1 Pro), and delusion co-construction (Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash, DeepSeek-V3, Claude Sonnet 4). The findings demonstrate that LLM safety for psychiatric populations must be evaluated longitudinally, as psychosis-enhancing factors emerge over extended interactions rather than in isolated responses.

benchmark_name: Deep Multimodal Wearable Sensor Fusion for Detection of Body-Focused Repetitive Behaviors
authors: Samaneh Rezaeimanesh; Mohsen Behradfar; Mohammad Fili; Guiping Hu
institutions: Department of Systems Engineering and Operations Research, George Mason University, Fairfax, VA 22030, USA
journal_venue: Preprint — arXiv (submitted to IEEE for possible publication)
ground_truth_source: CMI – Detect Behavior with Sensor Data dataset (Child Mind Institute / Kaggle competition); sequences labeled with gesture type (Target/Non-Target), gesture identity, orientation, behavior phase, sequence counter, and subject identifier
size_of_benchmark: 8,151 unique sequences from 81 participants (train: 5,810; val: 714; test: 1,627)
what_assessed_skills: Detection and fine-grained classification of body-focused repetitive behaviors (BFRBs) vs. non-BFRB gestures from multimodal wrist-worn sensor data; multimodal sensor fusion; spatio-temporal feature learning; model interpretability
tasks_assessed: Binary BFRB detection (Target vs. Non-Target); 9-class BFRB gesture classification (each BFRB gesture vs. grouped Non-Target); post-hoc interpretability via SHAP; hierarchical clustering of misclassification patterns
population_represented: 81 participants (adults and children) recruited through the Child Mind Institute's Healthy Brain Network; demographics include age, sex, handedness, height, and arm measurements
languages: Not applicable (sensor data, no natural language)
evaluation_method: Automated evaluation on held-out test set (1,627 sequences from 16 participants); metrics: F1 score, Precision, Recall, Specificity, ROC-AUC for binary and macro-averaged 9-class settings; SHAP-based feature attribution; hierarchical clustering of confusion matrices
llms_evaluated: None — study uses deep learning models (CNN-GRU, BiGRU autoencoders, MLP Meta-Learner), not LLMs
mental_health_conditions: Body-focused repetitive behaviors (BFRBs): trichotillomania (hair pulling), excoriation disorder (skin picking/pinching); associated with obsessive-compulsive and anxiety disorders
performance_scores: ALL-MODALITY binary: F1=0.985, Precision=0.977, Recall=0.992, Specificity=0.960, ROC-AUC=0.997; ALL-MODALITY 9-class macro: F1=0.700, Precision=0.709, Recall=0.704, Specificity=0.973, ROC-AUC=0.963; IMU binary F1=0.972; THM binary F1=0.945; ToF binary F1=0.960
short_summary: This paper proposes a multimodal deep learning framework for detecting and classifying body-focused repetitive behaviors (BFRBs) such as hair pulling and skin picking using wrist-worn sensor data from the Child Mind Institute's Helios device. The system fuses IMU, thermopile (THM), and time-of-flight (ToF) sensor streams via a hybrid CNN-GRU architecture with modality-specific autoencoder pretraining and a late-fusion MLP classifier. No LLMs are evaluated; instead, the framework competes against unimodal baselines (IMU-only, THM-only, ToF-only). Evaluation on a subject-grouped held-out test set uses F1, precision, recall, specificity, and ROC-AUC for binary and 9-class tasks. The multimodal model achieves F1=0.985 (binary) and macro F1=0.700 (9-class), outperforming all unimodal baselines, with SHAP analysis showing ToF and IMU as dominant modalities.
